name: Frontal lobe
summary: The largest lobe, everything in front of the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. From back to front it contains the primary motor cortex on the precentral gyrus, the premotor and supplementary motor areas, the frontal eye field, Broca's area in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus, and the vast prefrontal cortex (dorsolateral, orbitofrontal and medial) that plans, sequences, inhibits and motivates behavior. Its medial surface belongs to the ACA and its lateral surface to the MCA, and its lesions range from contralateral weakness to the personality change, apathy and disinhibition that families notice before doctors do.

anatomy.location: Anterior to the central sulcus and superior to the lateral sulcus on the convexity; the medial surface extends to the cingulate sulcus and the paracentral lobule; the orbital surface rests on the orbital roofs. The superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri are separated by the superior and inferior frontal sulci; the inferior frontal gyrus is divided into orbital, triangular and opercular parts.

subdivisions.name: Premotor cortex and supplementary motor area (area 6)
Paracentral lobule (medial)
subdivisions.note: motor and sensory cortex for the leg and perineum

relations.inferior: lateral sulcus, temporal lobe and orbital roof
relations.medial: falx cerebri and the opposite frontal lobe

function: Voluntary movement, speech production, gaze control, executive function, working memory, judgement, motivation, social behavior, and control of micturition.

bestView.label: frontal convexity at the level of the lateral ventricles
medial frontal surface and the orbital surface
superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri

imaging.normalAppearance: On axial slices the frontal lobes lie in front of the central sulcus, identified by the omega-shaped hand knob of the precentral gyrus; on sagittal images the medial surface shows the cingulate sulcus and the paracentral lobule. Frontal atrophy with a knife-edge pattern is characteriztic of frontotemporal dementia.

pathology.finding: Hemorrhagic contusions of the orbital and frontal poles after deceleration injury, with edema and later encephalomalacia.
Infiltrating T2-bright mass (glioma) or extra-axial enhancing dural mass (olfactory groove or parasagittal meningioma) with personality change and, if parasagittal, leg weakness.
Asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal atrophy sparing the posterior brain.
Restricted diffusion in the medial (ACA) or lateral (MCA) frontal cortex.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: MRI with T1, FLAIR and contrast; CT in trauma

lesionEffects.mechanism: Precentral gyrus and underlying corona radiata
Medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortex
Medial frontal cortex and its connections
Olfactory tract on the orbital surface compressed by a subfrontal mass

examination: Power, drift and fine finger movements
Frontal assessment: verbal fluency, Luria sequence, go/no-go, similarities
Primitive reflexes: grasp, palmomental, glabellar tap
Gait; ask about continence and personality change
pearls: Personality change with preserved memory is frontal until proven otherwise
A slowly growing frontal tumor can be silent for years; new-onset apathy or disinhibition in middle age deserves imaging

pitfalls: Frontal signs are easily mistaken for depression or dementia of other types
